data.title: Weak Account Passwords Recovered Through Password Spraying
data.summary:
Valid domain credentials were obtained by testing a small number of predictable
passwords against the full list of domain accounts, providing authenticated
access to the environment without exploiting any vulnerability.
data.description:
Password spraying attempts a small number of likely passwords against a large
number of accounts, rather than many passwords against one account. Because each
account receives only one or two attempts within a lockout observation window, no
account is locked and the activity does not trigger controls designed to detect
brute force attempts against individual users.

The account list required was obtained through directory enumeration, and the
password policy in force disclosed the minimum length, allowing candidate values
that would certainly fail to be excluded in advance. The passwords tested
followed patterns commonly adopted where complexity requirements are enforced
without a length requirement sufficient to make them impractical: a season or the
organisation's name combined with a year and a symbol.

Several accounts authenticated successfully using passwords of this type. Where
one of the accounts concerned held privileges beyond those of a standard user,
the attack provided elevated access directly rather than merely a foothold.

The attack needs no vulnerability, exploit code, or specialist tooling,
and produces authentication events indistinguishable from legitimate logons once
the correct password is found.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access and no prior credentials could obtain valid
domain accounts, providing the authenticated access required for directory
enumeration, share access, and the majority of the further attacks documented in
this report. Where an account with elevated privileges is among those recovered,
the attacker gains those privileges immediately.
data.recommendation:
1. Force a password reset for all accounts whose passwords were recovered, and
   review those accounts for evidence of prior unauthorised use.

2. Increase the minimum password length as described in the related finding on
   password policy, as length rather than complexity determines resistance to
   this attack.

3. Deploy a password filter that blocks organisationally predictable values,
   including the company name, product names, and seasonal patterns, at the point
   the password is set.

4. Enable multi-factor authentication on all externally reachable authentication
   endpoints, so that a recovered password alone does not grant access.

5. Configure alerting on authentication failures aggregated by source rather than
   by account, as spraying produces a small number of failures across many
   accounts and is invisible to per-account thresholds.

6. Restrict anonymous directory enumeration so that the account list required to
   conduct the attack is not available to unauthenticated parties.

data.title: Local and Remote File Inclusion
data.summary:
The application incorporated user-supplied values into file path operations
without validation, allowing arbitrary files to be read from the server and, in
some configurations, executed.
data.description:
The application selected files to include or display based on a value supplied in
the request. Because the value was neither validated against a fixed set of
permitted options nor constrained to an expected directory, traversal sequences
could be used to reference files elsewhere on the filesystem.

This permits the contents of arbitrary files readable by the application account
to be retrieved, including application source code, configuration files
containing database credentials, and operating system files that disclose user
accounts and service configuration.

Where the referenced file is processed by a server-side interpreter rather than
returned as text, the impact extends to code execution. An attacker who can place
content of their choosing anywhere on the filesystem (through an upload
function, a log file that records request data, or a session store) can then
cause that content to be executed by referencing it through the vulnerable
parameter.

Where the platform permits inclusion of remote resources, an attacker can supply
a URL under their control, causing the application to retrieve and execute
attacker-supplied code directly.
data.impact:
An attacker could retrieve the application's source code and configuration,
including credentials for databases and connected services, and enumerate the
operating system configuration. Where the conditions for execution are present,
this extends to arbitrary code execution on the server, resulting in complete
compromise of the host and a foothold within the internal network.
data.recommendation:
1. Avoid constructing file paths from user-supplied values. Where the request
   must select between files, map the supplied value to a fixed internal
   identifier through an allowlist, and reject anything not present in it.

2. Where a path must be constructed, resolve it to its canonical form and verify
   that the result falls within the intended directory before any file operation
   is performed. Filtering traversal sequences from the input is insufficient, as
   encoding variations defeat it.

3. Disable the inclusion of remote resources in the platform configuration, as it
   is rarely required and converts file inclusion directly into code execution.

4. Restrict the application account's filesystem access so that it can read only
   the directories it requires, limiting what is exposed should the controls
   above fail.

5. Store configuration files containing credentials outside the web root and with
   permissions restricting them to the accounts that require them.

data.title: Unsupported Operating System in Use
data.summary:
Systems were running operating system versions that have passed the end of their
support lifecycle and no longer receive security updates from the vendor,
leaving them permanently vulnerable.
data.description:
Hosts within the environment were running operating system versions for which
vendor support has ended. No security updates are issued for these products, so
any vulnerability discovered after the end-of-support date remains unaddressed
indefinitely.

This is not the same as a missing patch. A system missing an update can be
remediated by applying it; an unsupported system cannot be remediated at all,
because no fix exists or will be produced. The risk therefore increases
continuously over time as new vulnerabilities are discovered in the unsupported
codebase.

Unsupported versions also lack the security controls introduced in later
releases. Protections such as credential isolation, modern exploit mitigations,
and improved authentication handling are unavailable, so attacks that fail
against current systems succeed reliably against these hosts.

Because such systems are typically retained to support a legacy business
application, they are often connected to systems that hold current data,
providing an attacker with a route into the supported estate.
data.impact:
The affected systems cannot be secured against vulnerabilities discovered after
their end-of-support date and represent a permanent point of compromise within
the environment. An attacker reaching them could obtain complete control,
extract credential material, and use them as a stable foothold from which to
attack current systems, with the exposure increasing over time.
data.recommendation:
1. Migrate the affected systems to a currently supported operating system version
   according to a defined plan with committed dates.

2. Where the business application prevents migration, engage the vendor regarding
   a supported version, and where none exists, treat replacement of the
   application as a business risk decision requiring formal acceptance at an
   appropriate level.

3. As an interim control, isolate the affected systems on a dedicated network
   segment permitting only the specific connections the business function
   requires, in both directions.

4. Prevent privileged accounts from authenticating to these systems, as
   credential material exposed on an unsupported host cannot be adequately
   protected.

5. Where the vendor offers extended security updates commercially, evaluate the
   cost against the risk as a bridging measure, although such arrangements are
   time-limited and do not remove the need to migrate.

6. Maintain an inventory of operating system versions with their end-of-support
   dates, and review it in advance so that migrations are planned rather than
   reactive.

data.title: Missing Operating System Security Updates
data.summary:
Systems within the environment were missing security updates addressing
vulnerabilities for which reliable public exploit code exists, allowing remote
compromise without credentials.
data.description:
Hosts were identified running operating system builds that had not received
security updates released by the vendor. The absent updates addressed
vulnerabilities in network-facing services, several of which permit code
execution prior to authentication.

Exploit code for these vulnerabilities is publicly available, integrated into
widely distributed exploitation frameworks, and requires no specialist knowledge
to use. The interval between a patch being published and exploit code appearing
is routinely measured in days, so the exposure period represented by an unpatched
host is substantial.

Exploitation of the affected services typically yields execution in the context
of the operating system kernel or a highly privileged service account, meaning
successful exploitation results in immediate and complete compromise of the host
rather than a limited foothold requiring further escalation.

Affected systems were identified through service version
enumeration and confirmed where testing could be conducted safely.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to the affected systems could obtain complete
control of them without any credentials, using publicly available tooling. This
grants access to all data held on those hosts, permits the extraction of
credential material from memory including that of privileged users who have
logged on, and provides a position from which the remainder of the network can be
attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Apply all outstanding security updates to the affected systems as a
   priority, beginning with those addressing vulnerabilities in network-facing
   services that permit unauthenticated code execution.

2. Where a system cannot be patched within a reasonable period due to application
   compatibility, isolate it at the network level so that the affected services
   are reachable only from systems that genuinely require access, and document
   the exception with a review date.

3. Implement a patch management process with defined timescales by severity, and
   report against those timescales so that exceptions are visible to management
   rather than accumulating silently.

4. Deploy vulnerability scanning across the estate on a recurring basis and
   reconcile the results against the asset inventory, so that systems missing
   from patch management are identified.

5. Review the asset inventory itself, as unpatched systems are frequently those
   that no team recognises as their responsibility.

data.title: Default Credentials on Administrative Web Interface
data.summary:
Administrative web interfaces were accessible using vendor default credentials,
granting full control of the affected applications and, in several cases, command
execution on the underlying host.
data.description:
Applications exposing web-based management interfaces retained the
credentials assigned by the vendor at installation. These values are published in
product documentation and are held in publicly available wordlists, so no
guessing is required.

Administrative access to this type of application often extends beyond
the application itself. Build and automation platforms provide script execution
by design; application servers permit the deployment of arbitrary archives;
monitoring systems allow the definition of commands executed on managed hosts.
In each case, administrator access gives command
execution on the server.

Authentication performed with valid credentials produces no failed login events
and appears legitimate in application logs, so the activity is unlikely to be
detected by controls that monitor for authentication failures.

Successful authentication using default credentials was confirmed during testing.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to these interfaces could obtain full
administrative control of the affected applications without any prior credential
material. Where the application provides script or command execution
functionality, this results in code execution on the underlying operating system
and a foothold within the internal network, from which the wider environment can
be attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Change all default credentials immediately to values meeting the
   organisation's password standard, and review the affected applications for
   evidence of prior unauthorised access.

2. Where the application permits it, rename or disable the built-in
   administrative account rather than only changing its password.

3. Enable multi-factor authentication on all administrative interfaces where the
   application supports it.

4. Restrict network access to management interfaces so that they are reachable
   only from dedicated administrative networks, using host and network firewall
   rules rather than relying on the application's own access control.

5. Introduce a build review step that verifies default credentials have been
   changed and unnecessary management interfaces disabled before any system is
   placed into production.

6. Maintain an inventory of applications exposing management interfaces and audit
   it periodically, as such interfaces are frequently enabled by default and
   forgotten.

data.title: Operating System Command Injection
data.summary:
User-supplied input was incorporated into operating system commands without
sanitisation, allowing arbitrary commands to be executed on the underlying host.
data.description:
The application constructed operating system commands using values supplied in
the request, passing the resulting string to a system shell. Because shell
metacharacters were neither removed nor escaped, an attacker could terminate the
intended command and append commands of their own.

Execution occurs in the security context of the account running the application,
typically a service account with access to application configuration, connected
databases, and the local network. Where that account holds elevated privileges,
compromise of the host follows immediately.

The issue often arises in functionality that wraps a command-line utility,
such as network diagnostics, file conversion, archive handling, or report
generation. Input validation implemented on the client side offers no protection,
as requests can be submitted directly.

Command execution was confirmed during testing.
data.impact:
An attacker could execute arbitrary commands on the affected server, resulting in
disclosure of application source code, configuration, and credentials, access to
data held by the application and connected systems, and the ability to modify or
destroy that data. The compromised host also provides a position within
the internal network from which further systems can be attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Avoid invoking operating system commands from application code where a native
   library provides equivalent functionality. This removes the vulnerability
   class entirely rather than mitigating it.

2. Where a command must be invoked, use an interface that passes arguments as a
   structured array rather than as a single string interpreted by a shell, so
   that metacharacters carry no special meaning.

3. Validate all user-supplied values against a strict allowlist of permitted
   characters or against a fixed set of accepted options, rejecting anything that
   does not match.

4. Never construct commands through string concatenation of user input, and do
   not rely on escaping as the primary control, as escaping rules differ between
   shells and platforms.

5. Run the application under a dedicated low-privileged account and restrict its
   outbound network access, limiting what an attacker can achieve should
   execution occur.

data.title: Unrestricted File Upload Leading to Remote Code Execution
data.summary:
An upload function accepted files of arbitrary type and stored them in a location
from which the web server executed them, allowing arbitrary commands to be run on
the underlying host.
data.description:
The application provided a file upload function intended for documents and
images. No validation was performed on the file extension, the declared content
type, or the file signature, and uploaded files were written to a directory
within the web root that remained directly reachable over HTTP.

As a result, a file carrying an extension handled by the server-side interpreter
was executed rather than served as static content. This lets the uploader run arbitrary commands in the security context of the account under
which the web service runs.

Where validation is implemented solely on the client, it provides no protection,
as an attacker submits the request directly and never executes the client-side
code. Validation based on the declared content type is likewise ineffective,
since that value is supplied by the requester.

The issue was confirmed by uploading a file containing server-side code and
observing its execution.
data.impact:
An attacker could execute arbitrary commands on the web server, obtaining access
to the application's source code, configuration files, and any credentials they
contain, as well as the data held by connected systems. This establishes a
foothold within the internal network from which further systems can be attacked,
and represents complete compromise of the affected host.
data.recommendation:
1. Validate uploaded files against an allowlist of permitted extensions on the
   server side. Deny by default and permit only the specific types the business
   function requires; denylists are consistently bypassed.

2. Verify the file signature rather than relying on the extension or the declared
   content type, both of which are controlled by the requester.

3. Store uploaded files outside the web root and serve them through a handler
   that sets an appropriate content type and content disposition, so that the
   server never interprets uploaded content as executable.

4. Rename uploaded files to randomly generated values on receipt, discarding the
   original name, to prevent extension manipulation and path traversal.

5. Disable script execution in any directory that receives uploaded content
   through web server configuration, as a defence-in-depth control.

6. Run the web service under a dedicated low-privileged account with no rights
   beyond those it requires, limiting the impact should the controls above fail.

data.title: Default or Weak Service Credentials
data.summary:
Multiple internal services were accessible using default or trivially guessable
credentials, granting immediate administrative access to database and
application management interfaces.
data.description:
Several services exposed on the internal network were configured with vendor
default credentials or with passwords that were trivially guessable. These
accounts held administrative privileges within their respective applications.

In the case of database services, administrative access also permitted
operating system command execution through built-in functionality such as the
MSSQL xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure, turning application-level access
into host-level compromise.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to these services could authenticate as an
administrator without any prior credential material. Where the affected service
runs under a privileged account, this results in code execution on the underlying
operating system, compromise of the data the service holds, and a foothold from
which the wider domain can be attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Change all default and weak credentials immediately to values meeting the
   organisation's password standard, with a minimum of 15 random characters for
   service accounts.

2. Where the service supports it, disable or rename built-in default accounts
   rather than only changing their password.

3. Disable dangerous built-in functionality that is not required for operation,
   including the MSSQL xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure.

4. Restrict network access to management interfaces to dedicated administrative
   networks using host and network firewall rules.

5. Introduce a build review process that verifies default credentials have been
   changed before any system is placed into production.

data.title: SQL Injection (SQLi)
data.summary:
The web application processed user input in an insecure manner and was thus vulnerable to SQL injection. 
In an SQL injection attack, special input values in the web application are used to influence the application's SQL statements to its database. 
Depending on the database used and the design of the application, this may make it possible to read and modify the data stored in the database, perform administrative actions (e.g., shut down the DBMS), or in some cases even gain code execution and the accompanying complete control over the vulnerable server.
data.description:
We identified an SQL injection vulnerability in the web application and were able to access stored data in the database as a result.

The parameter `<PARAMETER_NAME>` in `<URL>` passes user input into an SQL statement without parameterization. We confirmed the injection by sending a single quote (`'`), which produced a database error, and then by sending boolean conditions (`' AND 1=1-- -` and `' AND 1=2-- -`) that changed the response content as expected. The back-end database is `<DBMS>`.

We then used a UNION-based payload to determine the column count and extract data from the database. The following request retrieved the current database user and version:

```http
GET <URL>?<PARAMETER_NAME>=' UNION SELECT NULL,user(),version()-- - HTTP/1.1
Host: <HOST>
```

Using the same technique we enumerated the schema through `information_schema` and dumped `<TABLE_NAME>`, which contains `<SENSITIVE_DATA>`. The tool `sqlmap` confirmed the finding and the injection type (`<BOOLEAN/UNION/ERROR/TIME>`-based).

SQL Injection is a common server-side vulnerability in web applications. 
It occurs when software developers create dynamic database queries that contain user input. 
In an attack, user input is crafted in such a way that the originally intended action of an SQL statement is changed. 
SQL injection vulnerabilities result from an application's failure to create dynamic database queries securely and to properly validate user input. 
They are based on the fact that the SQL language basically does not distinguish between control characters and data characters. 
In order to use a control character in the data part of an SQL statement, it must be encoded or escaped appropriately beforehand.

An SQL injection attack is therefore essentially carried out by inserting a control character such as `'` (single apostrophe) into the user input to place new commands that were not present in the original SQL statement. 
A simple example will demonstrate this process. 
The following SELECT statement contains a variable userId. 
The purpose of this statement is to get data of a user with a specific user id from the Users table.

```python
sqlStmnt = 'SELECT * FROM Users WHERE UserId = ' + userId;
```

An attacker could now use special user input to change the original intent of the SQL statement. 
For example, he could use the string `' or 1=1` as user input. 
In this case, the application would construct the following SQL statement:

```python
sqlStmnt = 'SELECT * FROM Users WHERE UserId = ' + ' or 1=1;
```

Instead of the data of a user with a specific user ID, the data of all users in the table is now returned to the attacker after executing the statement. 
This gives an attacker the ability to control the SQL statement in his own favor. 

There are a number of variants of SQL injection vulnerabilities, attacks and techniques that occur in different situations and depending on the database system used. 
However, what they all have in common is that, as in the example above, user input is always used to dynamically construct SQL statements. 
Successful SQL injection attacks can have far-reaching consequences. 
One would be the loss of confidentiality and integrity of the stored data. 
Attackers could gain read and possibly write access to sensitive data in the database. 
SQL injection could also compromise the authentication and authorization of the web application, allowing attackers to bypass existing access controls. 
In some cases, SQL injection can also be used to gain code execution, allowing an attacker to gain complete control over the vulnerable server.
data.recommendation:
* Use prepared statements throughout the application to effectively avoid SQL injection vulnerabilities. Prepared statements are parameterized statements and ensure that even if input values are manipulated, an attacker is unable to change the original intent of an SQL statement. 
* Use existing stored procedures by default where possible. Typically, stored procedures are implemented as secure parameterized queries and thus protect against SQL injections.
* Always validate all user input. Ensure that only input that is expected and valid for the application is accepted. You should not sanitize potentially malicious input.
* To reduce the potential damage of a successful SQL Injection attack, you should minimize the assigned privileges of the database user used according to the principle of least privilege.
* For detailed information and assistance on how to prevent SQL Injection vulnerabilities, see OWASP's linked SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet.
data.short_recommendation: Make sure that Prepared Statements and Stored Procedures (where possible) are used throughout the application. This prevents the originally intended action of an SQL statement from being manipulated by an attacker.

data.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
data.summary:
The application retrieved resources from URLs supplied in the request, allowing
an attacker to direct those requests at internal systems otherwise unreachable
from outside the network.
data.description:
The application accepted a URL as input and issued a request to it from the
server. Because the destination was not restricted, an attacker could supply
addresses referring to systems within the internal network, to the server itself
via its loopback interface, or to cloud platform metadata services.

Requests issued this way originate from the application server and therefore
carry its network position and, in some cases, its credentials. Controls that
restrict access based on source address treat the request as internal and permit
it. Services intentionally bound to the loopback interface on the assumption that
they are unreachable become accessible.

The technique permits the internal network to be mapped by observing differences
in response time and content between addresses that are reachable and those that
are not. Where the application returns the content retrieved, data from internal
services is disclosed directly; where it does not, the difference in behaviour
still reveals the state of the target.

Validation based on the hostname supplied is often insufficient, as
redirects, alternative address encodings, and DNS records resolving to internal
addresses each defeat it.
data.impact:
An attacker could reach internal systems from outside the network using the
application server as a relay, enumerate internal infrastructure, and interact
with services that rely on network position for their protection. Where cloud
metadata services are reachable, this may disclose credentials granting access to
the wider hosting environment.
data.recommendation:
1. Where the set of destinations is known, validate the supplied value against an
   allowlist of permitted hosts and reject anything else. This is the only
   reliable control.

2. Where arbitrary destinations must be supported, resolve the hostname and
   verify that the resulting address is not within private, loopback, or
   link-local ranges, repeating the check after every redirect rather than only
   on the initial value.

3. Disable redirect following and restrict the permitted schemes to HTTP and
   HTTPS, preventing the use of alternative protocol handlers.

4. Issue outbound requests through a dedicated egress proxy with its own
   allowlist, so that network controls enforce the restriction independently of
   the application.

5. Require authentication on internal services rather than relying on network
   position, and enforce the use of the instance metadata service version that
   requires a session token where the application is cloud hosted.

6. Return a generic response to the client rather than the content retrieved,
   where the business function permits.

data.title: Weak Active Directory Password Policy
data.summary:
The domain password policy permitted short passwords and did not prevent the use
of predictable or previously breached values, allowing a significant proportion of
account passwords to be recovered.
data.description:
The Active Directory password policy enforced a minimum length below current
recognised guidance and applied no restriction on commonly used or organisationally
predictable values. Complexity requirements alone do not prevent passwords that
follow predictable patterns such as a season or company name combined with a year
and a symbol.

Analysis of recovered password hashes showed widespread use of such patterns,
including among accounts holding elevated privileges.
data.impact:
An attacker could recover valid credentials through password spraying or offline
cracking of captured hashes. Because the affected accounts include privileged
users, this provides a route from no access at all to administrative control of
the domain, without requiring the exploitation of any software vulnerability.
data.recommendation:
1. Increase the minimum password length to at least 14 characters for standard
   accounts and 25 characters for privileged and service accounts.

2. Deploy a password filter or Azure AD Password Protection to block common,
   breached, and organisationally predictable passwords at the point of change.

3. Encourage the use of passphrases and deploy an approved password manager so
   that longer values remain practical for users.

4. Configure an account lockout threshold that mitigates online password guessing
   while accounting for the risk of denial of service, and monitor for spraying
   patterns across many accounts.

5. Conduct a periodic domain password audit against a breached-password corpus and
   force resets for any account whose password is recovered.

data.title: Active Directory Domain Trust Exploitation
data.summary: Trust relationships between Active Directory domains were exploited to escalate access from a compromised child domain to the forest root, granting administrative control over the entire forest.
data.description:
Active Directory forests can contain multiple domains connected by trust relationships. A parent-child trust is created automatically when a child domain is added and is bidirectional and transitive by default.

When an attacker has compromised a child domain and obtained the krbtgt hash (through DCSync or NTDS.dit extraction), they can forge a Golden Ticket that includes a SID History attribute containing the SID of the Enterprise Admins group in the forest root domain. This is known as the ExtraSids or SID History injection attack.

The forged ticket is accepted by the forest root domain controller because SID filtering is not enforced on intra-forest trusts by default. The domain controller treats the SID History entries as legitimate group memberships, granting the ticket holder Enterprise Admin rights across the entire forest.

Alternatively, the inter-realm trust key (the password hash of the trust account) can be extracted from either side of the trust and used to forge inter-realm referral tickets, achieving the same result.

This attack was used during the assessment to escalate from the compromised child domain to full administrative control of the forest root domain.
data.impact: Compromise of a single child domain was escalated to full administrative control of the entire Active Directory forest, including all domains within it. This granted access to every domain-joined system, all user accounts, and all data across all domains in the forest.
data.recommendation:
1. Enable SID filtering on all trusts where it is not enforced by default, particularly on external and forest trusts. Note that SID filtering is not applied to intra-forest parent-child trusts by design, so the primary defense is preventing child domain compromise.

2. Treat every domain in the forest as a trust boundary that depends on the security of all other domains. A domain with weaker controls lowers the security of the entire forest.

3. Protect the krbtgt account by resetting its password twice annually and monitoring for DCSync activity (replication from non-DC sources).

4. Restrict membership in Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins to temporary use only, removing members when the specific task is complete.

5. Consider deploying separate forests for environments with materially different security requirements, as intra-forest trusts cannot be fully hardened against this attack.

6. Monitor for Kerberos tickets containing SID History attributes, particularly those referencing high-privilege SIDs from other domains.

data.title: Lateral Movement via Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket
data.summary: NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets extracted from compromised hosts were used to authenticate to additional systems without knowing the plaintext password, enabling movement across the network.
data.description:
Windows NTLM authentication accepts the password hash directly during the challenge-response exchange. An attacker who extracts the NTLM hash of an account from a compromised host can authenticate as that account to any service that accepts NTLM, without ever recovering the plaintext password. This is commonly referred to as pass-the-hash.

Kerberos tickets (TGTs and service tickets) extracted from memory on a compromised host can be injected into a new logon session on the attacker's system. The injected ticket is then used to access services as the ticket owner. This is referred to as pass-the-ticket.

A variant called overpass-the-hash uses an NTLM hash to request a Kerberos TGT from the KDC, converting hash-based access into Kerberos-based access. This is useful when NTLM is restricted but Kerberos is available.

These techniques were used during the assessment to move between hosts after extracting credential material from compromised systems. The authentication events generated appear identical to legitimate logons and do not trigger failed-authentication alerts.

Tools used included Impacket (psexec.py, wmiexec.py, smbexec.py), CrackMapExec, and Rubeus for ticket operations.
data.impact: Compromise of a single host provided the credential material needed to authenticate to additional systems across the network. Each newly compromised host yielded further credentials, creating a chain of access that reached progressively more sensitive systems. The technique requires no password cracking and produces no failed authentication events, making it difficult to detect with standard monitoring.
data.recommendation:
1. Deploy Windows LAPS to ensure every host has a unique local administrator password, breaking the lateral movement chain for local accounts.

2. Add privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group, which prevents NTLM authentication and enforces Kerberos with non-exportable keys.

3. Enable Credential Guard on all supported systems to protect LSASS process memory from credential extraction.

4. Restrict administrative logons so that tier-zero accounts authenticate only to tier-zero systems, preventing their credentials from being exposed on lower-tier hosts.

5. Monitor for logon events where the authentication package is NTLM and the source is unexpected, and for Kerberos TGT requests from hosts that are not the account's usual workstation.

6. Disable NTLM authentication where possible using the Network Security: Restrict NTLM group policy settings, forcing Kerberos which provides better detection opportunities.

data.title: DCSync - Replication of Domain Credentials
data.summary: An account with directory replication rights was used to request the password hashes of all domain accounts directly from a domain controller, including the krbtgt account, without executing code on the DC itself.
data.description:
Active Directory domain controllers replicate credential data between each other using the Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol (MS-DRSR). Any security principal holding the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All extended rights on the domain object can invoke this protocol to request password data for any account.

Members of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and the domain controller computer accounts hold these rights by default. When an attacker compromises an account with these privileges, or when the rights have been delegated to a non-administrative account through misconfiguration, the attacker can replicate the NTLM hash and Kerberos keys of every account in the domain.

The attack was performed using secretsdump.py (Impacket) or the lsadump::dcsync module in mimikatz. The replication request is handled by the domain controller as a normal replication operation and does not require code execution on the DC, file access to NTDS.dit, or physical proximity to the server.

Recovery of the krbtgt hash allows the creation of Golden Tickets, granting persistent domain-wide access that survives password resets for all accounts except krbtgt itself. The krbtgt password must be reset twice (due to password history) to invalidate forged tickets.

Replication traffic from a non-DC source is a reliable indicator of this attack but is not monitored by default.
data.impact: The attacker obtained the password hash of every account in the domain, including all administrative, service, and user accounts. This grants the ability to authenticate as any user, forge Kerberos tickets for persistent access, and extract sensitive data protected by domain credentials. Recovery requires resetting the krbtgt account password twice and rotating all account credentials.
data.recommendation:
1. Remove replication rights from all accounts that are not domain controllers. Audit the domain object ACL for non-default entries holding Replicating Directory Changes or Replicating Directory Changes All.

2. Restrict Domain Admin membership to the minimum required accounts and treat every member as a tier-zero asset.

3. Deploy monitoring for replication requests originating from non-domain-controller sources. Event ID 4662 with the replication GUIDs identifies this activity.

4. Reset the krbtgt account password twice in succession to invalidate any Golden Tickets that may have been created, following Microsoft guidance for the reset interval.

5. Implement a tiered administration model so that accounts with replication rights are used only from hardened, dedicated administrative workstations.

6. Review all accounts compromised during this assessment and force credential rotation for every domain account, as the attacker held the ability to authenticate as any of them.

data.title: Insecure Kerberos Delegation Configuration
data.summary:
Systems and service accounts were configured with Kerberos delegation rights that
allowed authentication material belonging to privileged users to be captured and
reused.
data.description:
Kerberos delegation permits a service to act on behalf of a user when accessing a
further back-end service, a requirement for multi-tier applications. The security
of the mechanism depends heavily on which form of delegation is configured.

Where unconstrained delegation is enabled, any user authenticating to the affected
host has a copy of their ticket-granting ticket cached in the memory of that
system. An attacker holding administrative access to the host can extract those
tickets and reuse them to authenticate as the users concerned. The exposure is
not limited to services the host legitimately requires, as the cached ticket
grants access to any service in the domain.

An attacker can coerce a privileged system, including a domain
controller, into authenticating to the affected host, causing its ticket to be
cached and captured without waiting for a user to connect.

Where constrained delegation is configured with protocol transition, the account
may request tickets on behalf of any user without that user having authenticated
at all, extending the exposure to accounts that never interact with the service.

Hosts and accounts with delegation configured were identified within the
environment, and were not restricted by the mechanisms available to limit the
associated risk.
data.impact:
An attacker with administrative access to an affected host could capture and reuse
the authentication material of privileged users, including domain administrators,
without recovering any password. Where a domain controller can be coerced into
authenticating, this results in full domain compromise from a single compromised
server.
data.recommendation:
1. Remove unconstrained delegation from all accounts and computers. Where
   delegation is genuinely required, migrate to resource-based constrained
   delegation, which places control with the target resource rather than the
   requesting service.

2. Add all privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group and set the
   "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated" flag, which prevents their
   tickets from being delegated under any configuration.

3. Treat any host holding delegation rights as a tier-zero asset, applying the
   same hardening, monitoring, and administrative restrictions as a domain
   controller.

4. Disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and other systems
   where it is not required, as it is commonly used to coerce authentication.

5. Audit delegation configuration on a recurring basis, as the settings are
   frequently applied during application deployment and rarely reviewed
   afterwards.

data.title: Insecure Active Directory Certificate Services Template Configuration
data.summary:
A certificate template permitted standard domain users to request certificates on
behalf of any account, including domain administrators, allowing authentication
as those accounts.
data.description:
Active Directory Certificate Services issues certificates according to templates
that define who may enrol and what the resulting certificate may be used for.
Where a template permits client authentication, allows the requester to supply an
arbitrary subject alternative name, does not require approval by a certificate
manager, and grants enrolment rights to broad groups, the combination allows any
member of those groups to obtain a certificate identifying them as any other
account in the directory.

The resulting certificate is issued by the enterprise certification authority and
is therefore trusted for Kerberos authentication throughout the forest. The holder
can authenticate as the impersonated account without ever knowing its password.

This condition is particularly durable. A certificate remains valid for its full
lifetime regardless of password changes, so an attacker retains access even after
the compromised account's password is reset. Remediation requires revocation of
the certificate in addition to correcting the template.

A template meeting these conditions was identified within the environment and was
enrollable by standard domain users.
data.impact:
Any authenticated domain user could obtain a certificate authenticating them as a
domain administrator, resulting in complete compromise of the Active Directory
forest. Because the certificate remains valid independently of the account's
password, access persists through credential rotation and standard incident
response measures unless the certificate itself is identified and revoked.
data.recommendation:
1. Disable the affected certificate template immediately, or remove client
   authentication from its extended key usage where the template serves another
   legitimate purpose.

2. Remove the "Supply in the request" setting for subject alternative names.
   Certificate subjects should be constructed by the certification authority from
   directory data rather than supplied by the requester.

3. Enable certificate manager approval on any template that permits client
   authentication and is enrollable by non-administrative users.

4. Restrict enrolment rights to purpose-specific security groups, removing broad
   principals such as Domain Users and Authenticated Users.

5. Audit all certificates already issued from the affected template, and revoke
   any that cannot be attributed to a legitimate request. Correcting the template
   alone does not invalidate certificates already obtained.

6. Review all templates in the environment against known misconfiguration classes
   using a tool such as Certify or Certipy, as several distinct escalation paths
   exist beyond the one identified here.

data.title: Local Administrator Password Reuse
data.summary:
The built-in local administrator account shared an identical password across
multiple systems, allowing compromise of a single host to be converted into
administrative access across a large portion of the estate.
data.description:
Local administrator accounts on the affected systems were configured with the
same password, a condition that typically arises where hosts are deployed from a
common image and the built-in account is never subsequently rotated.

Once an attacker obtains administrative access to any single host, the password
hash of the local administrator account can be extracted from the local security
database. Because Windows accepts NTLM hashes directly for authentication, this
material can be reused against other systems without the plaintext password ever
being recovered, a technique commonly referred to as pass-the-hash.

Authentication performed this way is indistinguishable from legitimate
administrative activity at the protocol level, and succeeds on every host sharing
the password. A single compromised workstation therefore provides administrative
access to all similarly configured systems within the environment.

No password rotation mechanism was observed in place for these accounts, meaning
the exposure persists indefinitely and is unaffected by domain password policy,
which does not apply to local accounts.
data.impact:
Compromise of any single host would grant an attacker administrative access to
every other system sharing the local administrator password. This permits the
extraction of domain credential material from memory on each host reached,
including the credentials of privileged users who have logged on, providing a
direct path from a single low-value workstation to compromise of the domain.
data.recommendation:
1. Deploy Windows LAPS across all domain-joined systems. LAPS assigns a unique,
   randomly generated password to the local administrator account of each host
   and rotates it automatically on a defined schedule.

2. Change the shared password immediately on all affected systems as an interim
   measure, ensuring a distinct value is set per host.

3. Restrict access to LAPS-managed passwords through directory permissions so
   that only authorised administrative roles can read them, and enable auditing
   of password retrieval.

4. Enable the "Deny access to this computer from the network" and "Deny log on
   through Remote Desktop Services" policies for local accounts, which prevents
   remote authentication using local credentials and blocks lateral movement even
   where a password is recovered.

5. Disable the built-in local administrator account entirely on systems where a
   domain-based administrative model provides equivalent access.

6. Review the build and imaging process to ensure newly deployed systems are
   enrolled in LAPS before being placed into production.

data.title: Excessive Active Directory Object Permissions
data.summary:
Standard domain accounts held permissions over privileged Active Directory
objects that allowed them to reset passwords, modify group membership, and
ultimately obtain administrative control of the domain.
data.description:
Every object in Active Directory carries an access control list defining which
security principals may read and modify it. Rights such as GenericAll,
GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, and ForceChangePassword permit the holder to
take control of the object they are granted over.

Permissions of this type accumulate over time through delegation performed for
operational convenience, through membership of nested groups, and through
application installations that request broad rights. Because they are not
visible in the standard administrative interface without inspecting each object
individually, they routinely remain in place long after the original business
need has ended.

The environment was found to contain permission chains allowing standard accounts
to reach privileged objects through a sequence of such rights. Each individual
step appears to be a legitimate delegation; the risk arises from the chain as a
whole.

Exploitation requires no software vulnerability and no elevated privileges. The
attacker uses the directory exactly as designed, which makes the activity
difficult to distinguish from normal administrative work.
data.impact:
An attacker holding any standard domain account could escalate to full
administrative control of the Active Directory domain by following the permission
chain, without exploiting a software vulnerability and without triggering
controls that monitor for exploitation activity. This grants access to every
domain-joined system and the data it holds.
data.recommendation:
1. Review the access control lists of all privileged objects, including
   administrative groups, service accounts, domain controller computer objects,
   and the domain object itself, and remove rights not required for current
   operations.

2. Map existing permission chains using an attack path analysis tool such as
   BloodHound, and prioritise remediation of the chokepoints through which the
   greatest number of paths pass.

3. Delegate administrative rights through purpose-specific groups scoped to
   organisational units, rather than granting rights directly to individual
   accounts or to broad groups.

4. Implement a tiered administration model so that accounts used to manage
   workstations cannot be used to reach domain controllers.

5. Enable auditing of directory object modification and alert on changes to
   privileged group membership and to access control lists on sensitive objects.

6. Repeat the attack path analysis on a recurring basis, as new permissions are
   introduced continuously through normal operations.

data.title: Credentials Stored in Group Policy Preferences
data.summary:
Group Policy Preference files stored on the SYSVOL share contained passwords
encrypted with a publicly published key, allowing any authenticated domain user
to recover them in plaintext.
data.description:
Group Policy Preferences allow administrators to configure local accounts,
scheduled tasks, mapped drives, and services across the domain. Where a password
is supplied, it is stored in an XML file within the SYSVOL share in a field named
cpassword, encrypted using AES with a static key.

Microsoft published this key in 2012 alongside the MS14-025 update, meaning the
encryption provides no protection. Any account able to read SYSVOL - which by
design includes every authenticated user in the domain - can retrieve the file
and decrypt the password instantly using publicly available tooling.

Although the update prevents the creation of new preferences containing
passwords, it does not remove files created before it was applied. These files
therefore persist indefinitely unless explicitly located and deleted.

Files of this type were identified within the SYSVOL share, containing recoverable
credentials for local administrative accounts.
data.impact:
Any authenticated domain user could recover credentials for local administrator
accounts deployed across the estate. Because such accounts are frequently
configured identically on every host, a single recovered password commonly grants
administrative access to a large number of systems, enabling widespread lateral
movement and the extraction of further credential material from memory.
data.recommendation:
1. Search the SYSVOL share across all domain controllers for XML files containing
   the cpassword attribute and delete every file identified.

2. Change the password of every account exposed in this way, and review those
   accounts for evidence of prior unauthorised use.

3. Deploy Windows LAPS to manage local administrator passwords, which assigns a
   unique randomly generated password per host and rotates it automatically.

4. Ensure the MS14-025 update is applied to all systems used to author Group
   Policy, preventing new preferences containing passwords from being created.

5. Establish a recurring audit of SYSVOL content, as restored backups and
   migrated policies can reintroduce affected files after remediation.

data.title: Cleartext Credentials Stored in Files and Network Shares
data.summary:
Plaintext credentials were stored in configuration files and scripts located on
network shares readable by all authenticated users, allowing privilege
escalation without exploiting any software vulnerability.
data.description:
Application configuration files, deployment scripts, and documentation stored on
internal file shares contained credentials in plaintext. The shares hosting these
files were readable by the Domain Users group, meaning any authenticated account
in the domain could retrieve them.

Credential material of this type is frequently reused across multiple systems and
services. Because retrieval requires no exploitation and generates no failed
authentication events, this weakness is unlikely to be detected by monitoring
controls.
data.impact:
An attacker holding any valid domain account could obtain credentials for
privileged service and administrative accounts without exploiting a software
vulnerability. This provides a direct path to lateral movement and privilege
escalation, and where the exposed account holds elevated domain rights, to full
compromise of the Active Directory environment.
data.recommendation:
1. Remove all plaintext credentials from scripts, configuration files, and
   documentation stored on network shares.

2. Rotate every credential identified as exposed, and audit those accounts for
   signs of prior unauthorised use.

3. Store application secrets in a dedicated secrets management solution such as
   Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, or Windows Credential Manager, and retrieve
   them at runtime rather than embedding them.

4. Review share and NTFS permissions so that access is granted only to the groups
   that require it, following the principle of least privilege.

5. Implement periodic automated scanning of file shares for credential patterns
   using tools such as Snaffler to prevent recurrence.

data.title: Kerberoasting - Service Accounts with Weak Passwords
data.summary:
Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for
accounts that have a registered Service Principal Name (SPN). The ticket is
encrypted using the service account's NTLM password hash, which allows the hash
to be extracted and subjected to offline brute-force attacks without generating
authentication failures or account lockouts.

Several service accounts within the domain were configured with weak,
human-generated passwords. These passwords were successfully recovered offline
within minutes using a standard wordlist.
data.description:
Any authenticated domain user is able to request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS)
for any account that has a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered against it.
This is standard Kerberos functionality and requires no elevated privileges; the
Key Distribution Centre performs no authorisation check to determine whether the
requesting user should have access to the service in question.

The returned ticket is encrypted using a key derived from the password of the
account the SPN belongs to. An attacker can therefore extract the encrypted
portion of the ticket and attempt to recover the account's plaintext password
offline, without any further interaction with the domain. Because the cracking
takes place entirely on attacker-controlled infrastructure, the activity produces
no failed authentication events, does not trigger account lockout, and is unlikely
to be detected by monitoring controls.

Service accounts within the domain were configured with passwords that did not
meet the length required to resist offline attack. Where a ticket is issued using
the legacy RC4 encryption type, cracking is substantially faster than against
AES-encrypted tickets. Several accounts returned tickets whose passwords were
recovered within minutes using a standard publicly available wordlist.

The exposure is increased where affected accounts hold privileges beyond those
required by the service they support, as recovery of the password grants the
attacker those privileges directly.
data.impact:
An attacker holding any valid domain account - including a low-privileged
account obtained through phishing or password spraying - could recover the
plaintext password of a privileged service account. Where such an account holds
elevated rights, this results in full compromise of the Active Directory domain,
granting access to all domain-joined systems, file shares, and the data they
contain.
data.recommendation:
1. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA). gMSA
   passwords are 120 characters, randomly generated, and rotated automatically
   by the domain controller.

2. Where gMSA is not supported by the application, configure the service account
   password to a minimum of 25 randomly generated characters and document a
   rotation schedule.

3. Remove Service Principal Names from accounts that do not require them.

4. Remove all service accounts from privileged groups such as Domain Admins,
   Enterprise Admins, and Account Operators. Grant only the specific rights the
   service requires.

5. Enable AES encryption for Kerberos on service accounts and disable RC4 where
   compatibility allows.

data.title: Broken Access Control on Administrative Functionality
data.summary:
Administrative functionality was reachable by standard users because access
control was applied only in the user interface rather than enforced on the
requests themselves.
data.description:
The application presented different interface elements according to the
authenticated user's role, concealing administrative functionality from standard
users. The underlying endpoints, however, performed no role check of their own
and processed any authenticated request they received.

Because the interface is rendered by the client, its behaviour is under the
control of the user. An attacker who knows or discovers the address of an
administrative endpoint can issue the request directly, and the application
executes it. Endpoint addresses are commonly disclosed in client-side code,
predictable from naming conventions, or present in documentation.

The same weakness applied to role assignment itself, where the value determining a
user's privileges was accepted from the request rather than read from the
authenticated session, allowing a user to grant themselves elevated access.

No exploitation is involved. The attacker issues ordinary, well-formed requests
that the application is not entitled to accept, which makes the activity
difficult to distinguish from legitimate administrative use in application logs.
data.impact:
A standard authenticated user could perform administrative actions within the
application, including the management of other users' accounts and access to data
across the full user base. Where role assignment could be influenced, the user
could grant themselves persistent administrative access, and the resulting
activity would appear legitimate in the application's own audit records.
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce authorisation on the server for every request, verifying the
   authenticated user's role against the operation requested. Interface-level
   concealment is a usability measure and provides no security.

2. Implement the check centrally, applying it by default to all endpoints and
   requiring an explicit exemption for those intended to be public, so that new
   functionality is protected without further action.

3. Derive the user's role from the authenticated session on the server. Never
   accept role, permission, or identity values from the request.

4. Deny by default, so that an endpoint with no explicit authorisation rule
   rejects requests rather than accepting them.

5. Log all administrative actions with the identity of the user performing them,
   and alert on administrative operations performed by accounts not assigned that
   role.

6. Test each endpoint with a request issued by a standard user as part of the
   development process, rather than relying on the interface to demonstrate that
   access is restricted.

data.title: Insufficient Network Segmentation
data.summary:
The internal network permitted unrestricted communication between systems of
differing security requirements, allowing compromise of a single low-value host
to reach critical infrastructure without obstruction.
data.description:
Systems of materially different sensitivity were found to share unrestricted
network reachability. Workstations could reach domain controllers, database
servers, and management interfaces directly on their administrative ports, and no
filtering was observed between the segments concerned.

Network segmentation exists to ensure that compromise of one system does not
translate into access to the entire estate. Where it is absent, an attacker who
gains a foothold anywhere obtains the same network position as if they had
compromised the most sensitive system in the environment, and can enumerate and
attack every host without needing to defeat any further control.

The absence of segmentation also removes an opportunity for detection. Traffic
crossing a boundary can be inspected and alerted upon; traffic within a flat
network is typically neither logged nor examined, so lateral movement produces no
signal.

This condition amplifies every other weakness present. A vulnerability confined
to one segment represents a contained risk; the same vulnerability on a flat
network represents a route to complete compromise.
data.impact:
Compromise of any single host, including a low-value workstation reached through
phishing, would provide an attacker with unrestricted network access to critical
infrastructure including domain controllers and database systems. This removes
any requirement for the attacker to defeat further network controls, and
substantially reduces the likelihood that lateral movement is detected before the
environment is fully compromised.
data.recommendation:
1. Define network zones based on the sensitivity and function of the systems they
   contain, separating user workstations, general servers, critical
   infrastructure, and management interfaces.

2. Implement filtering between zones permitting only the specific traffic
   required by business function, denying all other traffic by default.

3. Place all administrative interfaces on a dedicated management network
   reachable only from authorised administrative systems, so that a compromised
   workstation cannot reach them.

4. Restrict communication between workstations, as direct workstation-to-workstation
   traffic is rarely required and is a primary mechanism of lateral movement.

5. Log and monitor traffic crossing zone boundaries, so that lateral movement
   attempts generate a signal that can be investigated.

6. Validate the effectiveness of segmentation through periodic testing, as rules
   added over time to resolve operational problems frequently erode the intended
   boundaries.

data.title: Local Privilege Escalation via Misconfigured Windows Services
data.summary:
Windows services were configured in a manner that allowed standard users to
control the code executed when the service starts, providing a route to
SYSTEM-level access on the affected hosts.
data.description:
Windows services typically run under the SYSTEM account, the highest privilege
level available on the operating system. Where a standard user can influence what
the service executes, that user can obtain SYSTEM privileges.

Several distinct misconfigurations produce this outcome. Where the service binary
or its containing directory is writable by non-administrative users, the binary
can be replaced. Where the service configuration itself is modifiable, the
executable path can be redirected. Where the path contains spaces and is not
enclosed in quotation marks, Windows attempts to execute each partial path in
turn, allowing an executable placed at a predictable location to be run instead
of the intended one. Where the service loads a library from a directory the user
controls, that library can be substituted.

In each case the attacker supplies content that the operating system executes
with SYSTEM privileges when the service next starts. Where the user can also
restart the service, or where the host reboots on a schedule, no further
interaction is required.

These conditions arise most frequently with third-party software installed
outside the standard program directories, where the installer applies permissions
inherited from the parent directory rather than setting them explicitly.
data.impact:
An attacker holding access to any standard user account on the affected systems,
including access obtained through a compromised application service, could
escalate to SYSTEM privileges. This permits the extraction of credential material
from memory including that of privileged users who have logged on, the
installation of persistence, and the disabling of endpoint security controls,
providing material with which to attack the wider environment.
data.recommendation:
1. Correct the permissions on service binaries and their containing directories
   so that write access is restricted to administrators and the SYSTEM account.

2. Review service configuration permissions and remove the ability of
   non-administrative users to modify service definitions.

3. Enclose all service executable paths containing spaces in quotation marks
   within the registry, ensuring the intended binary is resolved.

4. Install third-party software within the standard program directories, where
   appropriate permissions are applied by default, rather than in locations
   created at the filesystem root.

5. Audit service configuration across the estate on a recurring basis, as
   software updates and reinstallations frequently reintroduce the conditions
   after remediation.

6. Apply application control so that only approved binaries may execute,
   preventing substituted content from running even where permissions are
   incorrect.

data.title: Local Privilege Escalation via Sudo Misconfiguration
data.summary:
The sudo configuration permitted standard users to execute commands as root that
provide a route to an interactive shell, allowing complete control of the
affected hosts.
data.description:
The sudo configuration on the affected systems granted standard user accounts the
ability to run specific commands with root privileges. The intention in such
configurations is to delegate a narrow administrative task without granting full
administrative access.

The commands permitted, however, provide functionality that can be used to obtain
an interactive shell. A wide range of ordinary utilities offer this capability
directly or indirectly, including editors that can spawn subprocesses,
interpreters that execute arbitrary code, pagers that invoke a shell, archive
tools that execute filters, and any utility accepting a user-controlled
configuration file. Where such a command is permitted, the delegation is
equivalent to granting unrestricted root access.

The use of wildcards in the configuration extends this further, as the pattern
frequently matches argument combinations the author did not anticipate, including
paths that permit arbitrary files to be read or written as root.

Where the NOPASSWD directive is also present, escalation requires no knowledge of
the user's own password, so any compromise of the account - including through a
service running under it - immediately becomes full compromise of the host.

Escalation to root was confirmed during testing.
data.impact:
An attacker holding access to any affected user account could obtain complete
control of the host. This permits access to all data held on the system, the
recovery of credentials stored in configuration files and process memory, the
installation of persistence, and the modification of logs to conceal the
activity. Where credentials recovered are valid elsewhere, the compromise extends
beyond the affected host.
data.recommendation:
1. Review the sudo configuration on all systems and remove entries granting
   commands that can be used to obtain a shell or to read and write arbitrary
   files as root.

2. Verify each permitted command against a reference of known escalation
   techniques, such as the GTFOBins project, before including it in the
   configuration.

3. Avoid wildcards in command specifications. Where a task requires arguments
   that vary, implement it as a dedicated script owned by root and not writable
   by the delegated user, and grant sudo access to that script alone.

4. Remove the NOPASSWD directive except where a documented operational
   requirement exists, so that escalation requires the user's own password.

5. Enable sudo command logging and forward the logs to a central system outside
   the host, so that a compromise of the host does not permit the record to be
   altered.

6. Review delegations periodically, as sudo entries added to resolve a specific
   operational problem are rarely removed once the problem has passed.
affected_components: <HOSTNAME> (<IP>) - user <USERNAME> permitted to run <COMMAND> as root

data.title: Local Privilege Escalation via Impersonation Privileges
data.summary:
Service accounts on affected hosts held impersonation privileges that allowed any
compromised service context to escalate to full SYSTEM-level control of the
operating system.
data.description:
Accounts running web and database services on the affected hosts held the
SeImpersonatePrivilege right. This privilege permits a process to assume the
security context of a client that connects to it.

By coercing a privileged process to authenticate to an attacker-controlled named
pipe or COM endpoint, a low-privileged service context can capture and impersonate
the SYSTEM token. The technique requires no software vulnerability and no patch
exists, as the behaviour is by design; mitigation depends on configuration.
data.impact:
Any compromise of an affected service - for example through a web application
vulnerability - immediately becomes a full compromise of the host. SYSTEM access
permits the extraction of cached credentials and password hashes from memory,
installation of persistence, and disabling of security controls, providing the
attacker with material to move laterally through the network.
data.recommendation:
1. Review which accounts hold SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
   and remove the right from any account that does not strictly require it.

2. Run application and database services under low-privileged, purpose-specific
   accounts rather than built-in service identities where the application supports it.

3. Apply all available operating system security updates, as several coercion
   techniques used to trigger this escalation have been addressed by patches.

4. Deploy endpoint detection capable of identifying named pipe impersonation and
   anomalous token manipulation.

5. Reduce the likelihood of initial service compromise by remediating the
   application-level vulnerabilities documented elsewhere in this report.

data.title: Exposed Sensitive Files and Directory Listing
data.summary:
Web servers disclosed directory contents and served files not intended for public
access, including version control data, backups, and configuration files
containing credentials.
data.description:
Directory listing was enabled on the affected web servers, causing the contents of
directories without an index file to be returned to any requester. This removes
the need for an attacker to guess filenames and provides a complete inventory of
the material present.

Files not intended to be served were additionally reachable. These included
version control metadata, from which the full source code history can be
reconstructed; backup and temporary copies of source files, which are returned as
text rather than executed and therefore disclose their contents including
embedded credentials; and configuration files containing database connection
details and application secrets.

Material of this type accumulates through ordinary development and deployment
activity. Editors create backup copies, deployments leave version control
directories in place, and administrators place archives in the web root for
transfer and do not remove them.

The information disclosed frequently enables further attack. Source code reveals
the application's logic and validation, allowing weaknesses to be identified
without testing, and credentials recovered from configuration are commonly valid
for databases and other systems.
data.impact:
An unauthenticated attacker could retrieve the application's source code,
configuration, and backup data, disclosing credentials for databases and
connected systems. Access to source code substantially reduces the effort
required to identify further vulnerabilities, and recovered credentials
frequently provide direct access to systems beyond the web server itself.
data.recommendation:
1. Disable directory listing in the web server configuration globally, enabling
   it only where a documented business requirement exists.

2. Remove version control directories, backup files, archives, and any other
   material not required for the application to function from the web root.

3. Configure the web server to deny requests for file extensions and directory
   names associated with development artefacts, so that material reintroduced by
   a future deployment is not served.

4. Store configuration files containing credentials outside the web root, and
   rotate any credential identified as exposed.

5. Introduce a deployment process that publishes only the files the application
   requires, rather than synchronising a working directory, as this prevents the
   condition from recurring.

6. Scan the application's exposed content periodically for material of this type,
   as it is reintroduced readily through routine maintenance.

data.title: AS-REP Roasting - Accounts Without Kerberos Pre-Authentication
data.summary:
Domain accounts were configured without Kerberos pre-authentication, allowing
password material to be requested and cracked offline by an unauthenticated
attacker with no credentials of any kind.
data.description:
Kerberos pre-authentication requires a client to prove knowledge of its password
before the Key Distribution Centre will issue an authentication ticket. Where the
"Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" attribute is set on an account, this
check is skipped and the KDC will return an AS-REP message to any requester.

The returned message contains a portion encrypted with a key derived from the
account's password. An attacker requires only the account name to obtain it;
no valid domain credentials are needed, meaning this attack can be performed by
an entirely unauthenticated party with network access to a domain controller.

Because the recovered material is cracked offline, the process generates no
failed authentication events, does not increment the account lockout counter,
and remains invisible to controls that monitor authentication failures.

Accounts within the domain were identified with this attribute set. The password
of at least one such account was recovered offline using a publicly available
wordlist, indicating that the password did not meet the length required to resist
offline attack.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to a domain controller and no credentials could
recover the plaintext password of an affected account. This provides an initial
foothold in the domain without any prior access. Where the affected account holds
elevated privileges, the attacker gains those privileges directly, and where it
holds only standard access, the account still serves as the starting point for
further attacks that require authenticated domain access.
data.recommendation:
1. Enable Kerberos pre-authentication on all accounts by clearing the
   "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" attribute in Active Directory
   Users and Computers, or by setting the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag to false.

2. Where a legacy application genuinely requires the setting, document the
   business justification, restrict the account to the minimum privileges
   required, and assign it a randomly generated password of at least 25
   characters.

3. Audit the domain regularly for accounts with the attribute set, as it is
   frequently enabled during troubleshooting and never reverted.

4. Configure alerting on Kerberos event ID 4768 where the pre-authentication
   type is zero, which indicates an AS-REP request against an affected account.

5. Increase the domain minimum password length so that recovered material cannot
   be cracked within a practical timeframe.

data.title: XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
data.summary:
The web application processed XML documents in an insecure manner, which made it vulnerable to XML External Entity (XXE) Injection attacks. 
XXE Injection is a vulnerability in web applications that allows an attacker to interfere with the processing of XML documents by an XML parser. 
This attack can lead to disclosure of confidential data, denial of service, server-side request forgery, and other severe impact on the underlying system or other backend systems.
data.description:
We identified an XXE injection vulnerability in the web application. 
The XML parser allowed the definition of XXEs, which could create a malicious XML document. 
The XXE contained a URL that referenced an external domain. 
After the XXE was dereferenced by the parser, the web application interacted with this domain, which is evident from the DNS requests.
